parts.title: Sentence comprehension: Weekend train note
parts.instructions: Read the short email from a friend. Choose the best word for each gap (1-5).
parts.passage:
Hi Marcus,

I just got back from my weekend train trip along the coast, and I wanted to share a few tips before you go. Although the morning express was delayed by twenty minutes, I still [1] to catch the branch line at York. My friend Elena recommended booking a window seat on the left side, [2] gives you the best views of the cliffs. You should definitely [3] advantage of the two-for-one café voucher printed on the back of your paper ticket. Next month I am hoping to [4] off on a longer journey through the northern valleys with a rail pass. Let me know if you want to [5] me up on my offer to lend you my folding map!

Best,
Chloe

questions.explanation: 'Managed to catch' is followed by 'to + infinitive' and means succeeded in doing something difficult; 'succeeded' uses 'in + -ing' and 'achieved' takes a noun.
'Which' introduces a non-defining relative clause referring back to 'a window seat on the left side'.
'Take advantage of' is a fixed collocation meaning to make good use of an opportunity or offer.
'Set off on a journey' is the phrasal verb meaning to begin a trip.
'Take someone up on an offer' is a phrasal verb meaning to accept someone's offer.

parts.title: Text cohesion: A misty valley train ride
parts.instructions: The first sentence of the text is in the right place. Put the five sentences (A-E) into the correct order (gaps 1-5) to make a clear story.
parts.passage: Last Saturday morning, I boarded the eight-fifteen regional train to visit a quiet market town in the hills. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]
sentences: By the time we reached the final station at ten o'clock, the sun had cleared the clouds and the market square was buzzing with life.
Soon after leaving the city suburbs behind, the track began climbing beside a winding river covered in morning mist.
Because the carriage was nearly empty, I moved across the aisle so I could watch the sheep fields without glare on the glass.
Halfway up the valley, the train paused at a tiny stone platform where two hikers climbed aboard with muddy boots.
I had packed a flask of hot tea and a cheese roll, which made the slow journey feel far more relaxing than driving on a motorway.

gaps.explanation: Sentence E introduces the snacks packed for the trip and sets the relaxed tone right after boarding the train.
'Soon after leaving the city suburbs behind' describes the first stage of the route climbing into the misty valley.
Moving across the aisle to watch the fields clearly follows the scenery described as the train climbs beside the river.
'Halfway up the valley, the train paused...' marks the midpoint of the journey after settling into the window seat.
'By the time we reached the final station at ten o'clock...' concludes the journey upon arrival at the market town.

parts.title: Opinion matching: Weekend rail travel
parts.instructions: Four people (A-D) give their opinions about taking trains for short weekend trips. Match each statement (1-7) to the correct person. You can use each person more than once.

texts.title: Yusuf
texts.text: I used to drive everywhere for weekend breaks, yet I always arrived exhausted after sitting in Friday traffic jams. Taking the train completely changed that for me. Even on a three-hour ride, I can read a novel, stretch my legs, and step off right in the centre of town without hunting for a parking space. The only thing that bothers me is how confusing rail ticket prices can be if you forget to book weeks ahead.

texts.title: Grace
texts.text: For me, a slow local train is the best part of a weekend away, not just a way to get from A to B. Last month I took a tiny two-carriage line across the moors, and the guard even pointed out wild deer from the doorway. Still, I wish rural stations had better connections to local buses. Once I stepped off the platform, I had to wait fifty minutes in the rain for a lift into the village.

texts.title: Dan
texts.text: People often complain that train tickets are too expensive, though I find weekend rail travel quite affordable when you use a regional pass and pack your own sandwiches. Station cafés charge a small fortune for lukewarm coffee! What I really appreciate about trains is travelling with friends: four of us can sit around a table playing cards and chatting, which is impossible in a cramped car.

texts.title: Mei
texts.text: I started choosing trains over short domestic flights two years ago mainly to cut down my carbon footprint. At first I worried the longer journey would eat up too much of my Saturday, yet I quickly realised how calm I felt without airport security queues. My main tip is to travel light with a single backpack, because lifting heavy suitcases onto high overhead racks is awkward on crowded trains.

parts.title: Long text comprehension: The rise of slow train travel
parts.instructions: Read the article about slow rail journeys and weekend train travel. Match each paragraph (1-7) to the best heading (A-H). There is one extra heading that you do not need.

paragraphs.text: For decades, holidaymakers judged transport by a single rule: how fast it could carry them from home to a distant beach or capital city. Yet in recent years, a growing number of travellers have begun choosing the opposite approach. Instead of rushing through crowded airport terminals for a forty-minute flight, weekend visitors are stepping onto regional trains that wind slowly through valleys, stop at tiny stone platforms, and turn the journey itself into the main event of the break.

Railways were not always built for leisure. During the nineteenth century, engineers laid tracks across mountains and coastlines mainly to move coal, timber, and farm produce to busy ports. When motorways expanded in the nineteen-sixties, many of these quiet branch lines lost passengers and nearly closed. Today, however, those exact historic routes—crossing tall stone bridges and hugging rocky sea cliffs—have been rediscovered by walkers, cyclists, and photographers looking for views that no motorway can offer.

One reason slow rail trips appeal to modern workers is the rare chance to disconnect from constant hurry. On a motorway, a driver must concentrate on traffic lanes for hours, and on a budget flight, passengers spend half their time standing in security queues. On a regional train, once your ticket is checked, your time belongs completely to you. You can watch rain sweep across green hills, sketch in a notebook, or read a paperback without checking a clock.

Local economies along quieter railway lines are also seeing welcome benefits. Unlike high-speed express trains that roar past small towns without stopping, slow weekend services drop visitors directly onto village high streets. Passengers step off for an hour to buy fresh bread from a family bakery, browse a second-hand bookshop, or eat lunch at a station café before catching the afternoon train onwards. That steady flow of weekend visitors helps keep rural shops open all year.

At the same time, overnight sleeper trains are making a remarkable comeback across several countries. After years of being replaced by cheap airlines, night routes with comfortable bunks and breakfast trays are selling out weeks in advance. Travellers enjoy falling asleep as the train leaves one city and waking up to mountain scenery hundreds of kilometres away, saving the cost of a hotel night while avoiding the tired rush of an early-morning flight.

Environmental awareness plays a major role in this shift as well. Transport studies consistently show that an electric or modern diesel train produces far fewer emissions per passenger than a car or a short-haul plane. For travellers who love exploring new regions yet feel uneasy about air travel, switching to weekend rail trips offers a practical compromise. You do not have to give up seeing new places; you simply choose closer destinations and enjoy the slower pace.

Planning a memorable weekend by rail still takes a little care. Because rural lines sometimes run only once every two hours, missing a connection can leave you waiting on an empty platform until dusk. Experienced rail travellers advise checking Sunday timetables in advance, packing snacks for small stations without shops, and leaving space between connections. With a bit of flexibility, even an unexpected delay becomes part of the relaxed adventure.

headings: How former goods lines became scenic tourist routes
Why night trains are attracting travellers again
Practical tips for organising a smooth rail weekend
Why high-speed express trains are replacing rural buses
Stepping away from speed to enjoy the journey
A greener way to explore without giving up travel
Mental freedom compared with driving or flying
How stopping trains support small town businesses

gaps.explanation: Paragraph 1 contrasts the old focus on speed with travellers choosing slower regional trains where the journey itself is the main event.
Paragraph 2 explains how nineteenth-century lines built for coal and farm goods survived closure and are now loved for their scenic bridges and cliffs.
Paragraph 3 compares the mental freedom of relaxing on a train with the stress of motorway driving and airport security queues.
Paragraph 4 describes how slow trains drop visitors directly onto village high streets, helping bakeries, bookshops, and cafés stay open.
Paragraph 5 focuses on the comeback of overnight sleeper trains with bunks and breakfast trays that save a hotel night.
Paragraph 6 explains that trains produce fewer emissions than planes or cars, offering a greener way to explore closer destinations.
Paragraph 7 gives practical planning advice such as checking Sunday timetables, packing snacks, and leaving time between connections.

Nobody is rushing to a meeting with headphones clamped on. parts.title: Monologue comprehension
parts.instructions: Listen to two speakers giving short talks: first a travel writer about a coastal railway line (questions 1-2), then a station volunteer about restoring a rural waiting room (questions 3-4). Choose the best answer for each question.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: First, you will hear Ben, a travel writer, talking about a weekend journey along a historic coastal railway.

turns.speaker: ben
turns.text: Before I boarded the West Cliff branch line last autumn, readers warned me that the old two-carriage train had no Wi-Fi, no power sockets, and a very bumpy track. I expected that to bother me, since I usually type notes on my laptop while travelling. Instead, losing my internet connection forced me to look out the window for three straight hours, watching fishing boats bob in tiny harbours just metres below the railway wall. We paused for twenty minutes at a quiet seaside halt so an express train could pass. Rather than complaining, half the passengers stepped onto the sunny platform to buy warm scones from a tiny wooden kiosk. That unplanned stop reminded me why slow rail travel feels so refreshing: you stop treating every minute like a race and start noticing the small towns you pass through.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Now you will hear Mei, a local volunteer, talking about turning an empty village station building into a weekend travel hub.

turns.speaker: mei
turns.text: Our village railway station still had trains stopping every hour, yet the Victorian brick ticket office had stood locked and dusty for nearly fifteen years. Everyone assumed it would cost a fortune to repair the roof and repaint the wooden benches. Once we opened the shutters, though, the stonework was surprisingly dry and solid. Our hardest job wasn't the building work at all — it was persuading commuters and weekend hikers that the space was actually open to use rather than private property. Things changed only after we put a bright chalkboard outside advertising free walking maps and hot tea for arriving passengers. Now cyclists leave muddy boots on the porch, locals swap paperbacks on the shelves, and my main advice to other village groups is to start with one welcoming weekly event rather than waiting until every room looks perfect.

Tell me what you see in these two photographs and compare the two travel experiences. Then answer these two questions:
1. What are the advantages of travelling on a quiet regional train compared with driving on a busy motorway?
2. Which way of travelling would you choose for a weekend trip, and why?

parts.title: Personal experience and discussion
parts.instructions: You have 1 minute to prepare and 2 minutes to speak continuously. Answer all three questions in one organised talk.

topics.prompt:
Talk about a memorable journey or weekend trip you took. Answer all three questions in one 2-minute talk:
1. Tell me about a memorable journey or weekend trip you have been on.
2. How did you feel during the trip, and what made it memorable?
3. Why do you think slow travel is becoming more popular than rushing to see many places?
